summary: Background: Diagnostic examination scheduling is a recurrent operational challenge in health care because limited daily capacity must be allocated across heterogeneous requests with different urgency and follow-up timing requirements. In this context, optimization methods can support more timely and efficient scheduling decisions. Objective: In collaboration with Unidade Local de Saúde de Santo António, an optimization-based approach was proposed to improve the management of outpatient examination scheduling. Methods: Anonymous operational data from Unidade Local de Saúde de Santo António, corresponding to 2025, were analyzed to model the scheduling process over a 4-week (28-d) horizon comprising 2460 examination requests, including 156 examinations with follow-up requirements. Two optimization approaches, Constraint Programming Satisfiability (CP-SAT) and a neural combinatorial optimization (NCO)–inspired constructive approach, were evaluated under the same daily capacity structure, prioritization logic, and penalty-based framework, confirmed across 10 independent runs under 4 solver configurations, with operational outcomes remaining unchanged. The best-performing approach was then compared with the hospital scheduling solution for the same period. Results: CP-SAT achieved the best overall performance among the 2 optimization approaches. It scheduled 1400 examinations vs 1391 for the NCO-inspired approach, reduced free time from 42 to 3 minutes, and achieved a substantially lower total penalty (49,790.78 vs 83,652.10). Both methods achieved 0 unscheduled due examinations, 0 delayed scheduled examinations, and 0 delayed unscheduled examinations. The NCO-inspired approach required less runtime than CP-SAT (17.2 vs 214.6 s). When compared with the hospital scheduling solution, CP-SAT scheduled more examinations (1400 vs 1147) and eliminated all unscheduled due examinations (0 vs 80), delayed scheduled examinations (0 vs 23), and delayed unscheduled examinations (0 vs 40). Conclusions: Both optimization approaches generated feasible schedules under the same evaluation framework, but CP-SAT produced the best overall results in the tested setting. The findings suggest that optimization-based scheduling can improve the timely allocation of diagnostic examinations and reduce follow-up–related delays when compared with routine hospital scheduling practice.
title: Constraint Programming and Neural-Inspired Optimization for Hospital Diagnostic Examination Scheduling: Comparative Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Autism spectrum disorder (ASD or autism) diagnosis faces significant delays due to specialist shortages and subjective, clinic-based assessments. Although AI offers a potentially scalable solution via automated video analysis, current state-of-the-art deep learning models often fail to capture subtle, clinically nuanced social behaviors essential for reliable detection. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and evaluate a human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that combines automated AI feature extraction with crowdsourced human annotation for autism classification on naturalistic home videos. We targeted low-confidence AI facial feature extraction outputs to be replaced by human features. We also sought to quantify the relationship between the confidence threshold used for swapping AI features with human features, the volume of human replacement of AI features, and the predictive diagnostic performance. <strong>Methods:</strong> We implemented a HITL pipeline integrating deep learning models for facial emotion (7-class) feature extraction. A confidence threshold applied to the emitted probability of the AI feature extractor model was used to identify low-confidence facial features or those that the AI model was unable to make a prediction for (henceforth referred to as “unresolved”), which were then replaced by human “feature extraction” (ie, annotation) conducted by rigorously vetted crowd workers. We evaluated this approach on 100 high-quality videos (50 autism and 50 neurotypical) from the GuessWhat? digital therapeutic app. Performance was assessed across decision thresholds (0.1-0.9 in increments of 0.1) using sensitivity, specificity, <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), with 5-fold cross-validation. <strong>Results:</strong> Across decision thresholds, performance improved overall but was nonmonotonic at intermediate thresholds. At a threshold of 0.9, 59.7% (597/1000) of frames were replaced by human annotations, and mean sensitivity increased from 0.51 (SD 0.24) at a threshold of 0.1 to 0.66 (SD 0.10) at a threshold of 0.9, an absolute increase of approximately 15 percentage points. The HITL-enhanced multimodal model achieved an aggregate out-of-fold AUROC of 0.76, compared with 0.54 for the AI-only model. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> In this proof-of-concept study, replacing AI features with human features tended to be associated with higher observed autism classification performance in this particular dataset. We targeted low-confidence and unresolved frames for human annotation. We note that these findings are exploratory and thus do not isolate the independent causal effect of human replacement or establish clinical diagnostic validity.
title: Balancing Human and AI Features for Digital Autism Diagnostics from Home Videos: Human-In-The-Loop Machine Learning Study

summary: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are ubiquitous in the health AI literature, yet are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This viewpoint does not attempt to define the 3 terms. It asks a prior, meta-level question: what kind of claim do we make when we call a system transparent, explainable, or interpretable? I argue that the 3 terms pick out 3 different kinds of claim. A transparency claim is structural: it concerns what can be inspected about a system. An explainability claim is relational: it concerns whether understanding is successfully conveyed to a specified class of observer. An interpretability claim is functional: it concerns whether a bounded human agent can, in principle, rederive the system’s output by following its procedure. I use the framing example of a clinical decision support system that uses machine learning to identify patients at risk of deterioration. I develop each claim type through competing technical accounts, consider salient objections to each, and defend the taxonomy against them. I close by drawing out what the taxonomy implies for the design, evaluation, reporting, and regulation of health AI, and for physician autonomy at the point of care.
title: What Kind of Claims Are Transparency, Explainability, and Interpretability? A Definitional Taxonomy for Health AI

summary: Background: Continuous, noninvasive blood pressure (BP) monitoring is clinically important for managing hemodynamic instability in the intensive care unit (ICU). However, current ICU practice primarily relies on invasive arterial catheterization. While this is the clinical gold standard for continuous measurement, it carries risks such as infection and thrombosis and is typically limited to select critical care settings. Objective: To reduce reliance on invasive arterial lines, we developed an interpretable estimation framework for systolic blood pressure (SBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) from single-sensor photoplethysmography (PPG). Methods: Synchronized PPG and arterial line 10-minute recordings from 100 patients in the ICU were analyzed. Using a hybrid feature selection strategy (RReliefF and intrinsic model–specific rankings), we reduced 201 initial features to an optimized subset of 30 core features. Model development and evaluation were designed to minimize information leakage and overfitting, incorporating nested cross-validation and patient-wise testing to assess generalizability across heterogeneous ICU populations. We developed and validated predictive models using machine learning techniques, specifically XGBoost (XGB), random forest, and support vector regression, with XGB serving as our primary model. Results: Among the evaluated models, the Hybrid Top 30 XGB configuration provided the best balance between estimation performance, model compactness, and computational efficiency. The model achieved mean absolute errors of 8.61 mm Hg (SBP), 3.50 mm Hg (MAP), and 2.62 mm Hg (DBP). For MAP and DBP, mean difference (SD) values of −0.09 (4.54) mm Hg and −1.07 (3.51) mm Hg, respectively, satisfied the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation numerical criteria, while performance corresponded to Grade A according to the British Hypertension Society grading criteria. Although SBP exhibited greater variability, estimation performance was largely preserved using a physiologically informed subset of 30 features (approximately 15% of the original feature set). Feature importance analysis revealed distinct physiological feature patterns across SBP, MAP, and DBP estimation. Conclusions: Interpretability analysis identified key predictors associated with wave reflection, systolic timing, low-frequency vasomotor activity, and autonomic regulation. By explicitly linking predictive features to underlying cardiovascular physiology, the proposed framework addresses a key limitation of existing black-box cuffless BP models. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that an optimized XGB framework using physiologically informed PPG features can provide accurate and computationally efficient BP estimation in ICU settings and may support the assessment of clinically relevant hemodynamic states using a single-sensor PPG platform. These findings provide a foundation for future development of more robust and generalizable interpretable BP estimation models and cuffless monitoring technologies.
title: Blood Pressure Estimation for Hemodynamic Monitoring Using Reduced Photoplethysmography Features in Intensive Care Units: Prospective Machine Learning Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Health systems are increasingly deploying patient-facing conversational AI platforms, yet validated methodologies for safety evaluation under realistic high-risk conditions are lacking. Prior work has documented safety failures in clinical AI but not shown whether iterative, health system–embedded testing can produce measurable safety improvement. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to evaluate a structured red teaming methodology for the safety assessment of a patient-facing clinical AI platform and determine whether targeted remediation guided by initial testing reduced safety failures in subsequent rounds of high-risk evaluations. <strong>Methods:</strong> A 2-phase prospective simulation study was conducted at a single academic health system in January and February 2026. Phase 1 enrolled 48 health care professionals who completed 6 randomized clinical scenarios (3 medium risk and 3 high risk). Following independent platform remediation informed by aggregated phase 1 findings, phase 2 enrolled 27 additional participants who completed 8 targeted high-risk scenarios. All 476 transcripts were independently scored by 3 calibrated raters using a 5-domain safety rubric. A strict firewall separated the research team from the platform developer, and only aggregated, deidentified findings were shared between phases. <strong>Results:</strong> In phase 1, the high-risk failure rate was 30.2% (35/116) of transcripts vs 5.6% (7/126) for medium-risk scenarios. In phase 2, the high-risk failure rate was 8.5% (20/234), representing an absolute difference of 21.7 percentage points (participant-clustered 95% CI 11.1-32.2) and a 72% relative difference, with comparable performance across prespecified and improvised prompts within the targeted failure categories. Interrater reliability was moderate to strong in phase 1 (intraclass correlation coefficient=0.66, 95% CI 0.62-0.69) and moderate in phase 2 (intraclass correlation coefficient=0.49, 95% CI 0.43-0.55). Agreement on the binary failure classification remained stable between phases (Fleiss κ=0.70 in both phases), with observed agreement increasing from 90.9% (220/242) to 94.9% (222/234). Residual failures clustered around triage calibration errors and scope violations. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Structured iterative red teaming was associated with improved safety performance on new high-risk scenarios following targeted remediation. The 5-domain rubric and scenario taxonomy offer a replicable methodology for health systems conducting predeployment and ongoing clinical AI safety assessment.
title: Red Teaming a Patient-Facing Clinical AI Platform: 2-Phase Prospective Study

summary: Background: People share health experiences online as stories, not isolated facts. Most computational systems reduce these narratives to keywords or claims, overlooking the agency, causality, and interpretation that determine whether health information is safe or potentially harmful to act on. Content can use medically accurate terminology while describing unsafe behavior, rendering it invisible to fact-checking and keyword approaches. This limitation, which we term , constrains the ability of computational systems to extract, represent, and reason over narratives as coherent wholes. Objective: This study introduces the Narrative Builder, a computational framework that reconstructs unstructured online health stories into machine-readable agent-action-outcome (AAO) narrative graphs, preserving structural, causal, and interpretive dimensions. We formalize narrative blindness as a measurable property of natural language processing systems and evaluate whether theory-grounded reconstruction can address it. Methods: We operationalized Labov and Waletzky’s sociolinguistic narrative theory within a computational AAO schema, enriched with interpretive dimensions from psychological and clinical communication frameworks. From 5386 Reddit health threads (spanning February 2019 to November 2024), 2 domain experts (a biomedical researcher and a physician) annotated a gold-standard dataset of 2000 segments from 704 threads, with interrater reliability (Krippendorff α) of 0.75 to 0.82 across all annotated tasks (0.78-0.81 for the 4 interpretive classification tasks). A dual-model architecture combining BioBERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations From Transformers for Biomedical Text Mining) with a conditional random field (CRF) layer for AAO extraction and multitask DistilBERT for interpretive classification was evaluated using 5-fold grouped cross-validation, grouped on the annotation-level key to prevent data leakage, with a separate held-out test set and a McNemar test against term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and BioBERT-without-CRF baselines. Results: The Narrative Builder achieved a span-level -score of 0.850 for AAO extraction on the held-out test set, with per-type of 0.90 (action), 0.83 (agent), and 0.77 (outcome), outperforming the TF-IDF baseline (0.781; <.001). Labovian stage classification reached macro- of 0.501, and interpretive dimensions reached macro- values of 0.466 (emotion), 0.528 (stance), and 0.465 (tone). Clinical-value extraction achieved a precision of 0.90, and Unified Medical Language System concept normalization reached 100% coverage across 12,101 queries. A rule-based causal direction classifier identified 17.3% of segments as candidate outcome-to-action (inverted) patterns, though validation showed limited precision (0.277), and this distribution is reported as exploratory. Single-rater expert review of generated graphs indicated narrative coherence (mean 0.89, SD 0.08) and medical plausibility (mean 0.91, SD 0.07). Conclusions: The Narrative Builder reads health stories as coherent wholes rather than isolated facts, producing AAO narrative graphs that retain the agents, actions, outcomes, and emotional framing that determine how individuals interpret and act on health information. By formalizing narrative blindness as a measurable property and reconstructing narrative structure with strong extraction performance, this work establishes narrative reconstruction as a feasible complement to fact-based health informatics, providing structured input for downstream credibility assessment.
title: AI-Driven Reconstruction of Online Health Narratives Using Agent-Action-Outcome Modeling: Algorithm Development and Validation

summary: Background: Pediatric influenza is an important public health concern. Chinese patent medicines are used in its treatment, but relevant clinical evidence is dispersed across guidelines, expert consensus statements, and clinical studies. The multidimensional knowledge required for syndrome-based prescribing complicates information retrieval and standardized clinical use. Objective: This study aimed to develop a traceable knowledge graph of Chinese patent medicines for pediatric influenza, integrate it with a large language model (LLM) to support evidence-based question answering, and evaluate answer quality and preliminary usability. Methods: We systematically searched for clinical practice guidelines, expert consensus statements, and clinical studies. Evidence segmentation, ontology development, LLM-assisted extraction with manual verification, terminology normalization, and knowledge integration were used to construct a Neo4j knowledge graph. Structured graph retrieval was combined with retrieval-augmented generation to develop a question-answering system. A standalone LLM and the knowledge graph–enhanced LLM (KG-LLM) each answered 80 standardized questions. Three clinical experts independently evaluated anonymized, randomly ordered answers for core task accuracy, completeness, and unsupported factual content. Five physicians participated in an exploratory usability evaluation using the System Usability Scale (SUS), study-specific Likert items, and self-reported evidence-location outcomes. Results: We included 142 publications and generated 1294 evidence units. The knowledge graph contained 3211 nodes and 19,671 relationships, linking structured knowledge to evidence units and source publications. Across 80 paired questions, KG-LLM achieved higher accuracy scores than the standalone LLM (mean 3.05, SD 1.88 vs mean 2.02, SD 1.54; Holm-adjusted <.001) and higher completeness scores (mean 3.11, SD 1.84 vs mean 2.42, SD 1.62; adjusted =.002). Among 78 pairs with determinate assessments, unsupported factual content was identified in 11 standalone LLM answers (14.1%) and no KG-LLM answers (0/78, 0%; adjusted =.002). The mean SUS score was 96.50 (SD 2.85). Of 5 physicians, 4 (80%) reported locating both the original publication and the corresponding evidence. Conclusions: The traceable knowledge graph and graph-enhanced question-answering system integrated clinical evidence on Chinese patent medicines for pediatric influenza. KG-LLM achieved higher accuracy and completeness and less unsupported factual content on standardized tasks than the standalone LLM. Preliminary usability findings were favorable, but generalizability, long-term usability, and safety in clinical practice require further evaluation.
title: A Knowledge Graph–Enhanced Question-Answering System for Chinese Patent Medicines in Pediatric Influenza: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Retrieval-augmented generation over clinical text depends on the embedding model chosen—a choice that interacts with documentation genre. Cross-site stability of embedding-model rankings has not been evaluated on real electronic health record (EHR) narratives with genre held constant; public benchmarks are predominantly single-source, and multi-institution evaluations compare models and query formulations within tasks rather than ranking stability across institutions. <strong>Objective:</strong> The aim of the study is to test whether embedding model rankings transfer across 2 institutional EHR corpora, with genre held constant; to examine the contributions of model, site/corpus, and genre and their dependence on scoring; and to test whether the dominant contributor depends on model-panel composition. <strong>Methods:</strong> We compared 13 embedding models on a known-item passage-to-source-document task, each query a deterministic 2-sentence excerpt from its target, in a 2×2 design crossing site/corpus (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center via MIMIC-IV-Note [Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Clinical Notes Module] and University of California, San Francisco via ER-Reason) with genre (discharge summary and imaging report). Query sentences were removed from their targets before indexing to prevent verbatim overlap, notes were deduplicated after normalization, models used their recommended pooling, long documents were scored as overlapping chunks by maximum similarity, and cell sizes were matched (N=1235 per cell). Effectiveness was measured by mean reciprocal rank at 10, rank transfer by Kendall τ and selection regret, and variance by factorial decomposition (η<sup>2</sup>). Transfer, regret, and the contrastive-panel decomposition carry 95% patient-clustered bootstrap intervals. <strong>Results:</strong> Among the 8 contrastive models, cross-site Kendall τ was 0.86 (95% CI 0.64-1.00) for discharge and 0.64 (95% CI 0.36-0.86) for imaging. The model×site interaction was small under every scoring choice (η<sup>2</sup>=0.005-0.029); the site/corpus main effect was negligible under best-chunk scoring (η<sup>2</sup>=0.000) but scoring-dependent (0.172 under mean-pooling). Cross-site selection regret was 0 for imaging and up to 0.033 for discharge (~10% of the destination’s best mean reciprocal rank; intervals 0-0.071). Adding 5 nonretrieval masked-language-model comparators moved the largest term to model (η<sup>2</sup>=0.874): the dominant-factor question is panel-sensitive, while the qualitative transfer conclusion was unchanged. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> For known-item retrieval from clinical notes at 2 US academic medical centers, embedding-model rankings showed positive cross-site concordance, moderate for imaging and strong for discharge summaries—with intervals wide enough that direction, not magnitude, is the finding. Which factor dominates absolute effectiveness depends on the panel evaluated: primary contrastive-panel scoring favors genre, whereas adding nonretrieval comparators makes model choice dominant; so, claims about major determinants are panel-specific. Cross-site model selection incurred zero to modest performance loss. When documentation genre and retrieval configuration are matched, model-selection results from one institutional EHR corpus may be a useful starting point for another, although local confirmation remains warranted. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong>
title: Cross-Site Stability of Embedding Model Rankings for Known-Item Retrieval From Clinical Notes: Two-Corpus Comparative Evaluation Study

summary: Race, ethnicity, online health information sharing, and AI-mediated environments can intersect in ways that may importantly shape individuals’ willingness to share health data with researchers. In this Viewpoint, we closely examine this intersection by drawing parallels between historical and contemporary public health controversies and discussing recent empirical work centered on privacy-related experiences, data donation, and emerging evidence on AI-mediated digital disenfranchisement. We describe how AI-driven online engagement centered on race, ethnicity, and health can facilitate mutual aid and peer support while also posing privacy, reputational, algorithmic, and psychosocial risks when improperly mediated. These effects, alone or combined, can erode trust in digital health research and other engagement initiatives. Therefore, we propose 2 complementary sets of evaluation metrics in response: one focused on how race-related online experiences influence trust, consent behavior, and participation in data sharing and the other focused on race-conscious AI performance within the scope of fairness, representation, and downstream health outcomes. Together, these metrics position race and ethnicity as a key analytic dimension, rather than an optional covariate, to guide teams focused on understanding race as a key analytic dimension in AI-enabled, health-related social engagement online and its full role in and impact on health research.
title: Understanding Race as a Key Analytic Dimension in AI-Enabled, Health-Related Social Engagement Online and Its Role and Impact in Health Research

summary: Background: Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective: This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods: In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results: Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment (=0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment (=−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust (=.04), joy (=.01), sadness (=.004), surprise (=.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions: In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.
title: Detecting Emotional Signals of Relationship Well-Being Using AI: A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Transformer-Based and Lexicon-Based Models for Couples Therapy Research
